rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque notice period demand payment within thirty days
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 notice to drawer
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 cause of action
rows.answer:
A payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a written notice to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned unpaid, as provided in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. The drawer is then given fifteen days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment before a complaint can be filed [1]. As discussed by the Supreme Court in Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey & Anr., a complaint filed before the expiry of the 15 days is premature and the cause of action has not arisen [11]. Furthermore, as noted by the Supreme Court in Kamlesh Kumar v. State of Bihar & Anr., after the notice is sent and the 15 days' time to pay expires upon failure of the noticee, the complainant has one month from that cause of action to file the complaint [12].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within six months from its date or within its period of validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The written notice demanding payment must be given within thirty days of the payee or holder in due course receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned unpaid [1]

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to consideration for negotiable instruments
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
rows.answer:
Until the contrary is proved, it is presumed that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

As discussed by the Supreme Court in K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr., once the plaintiff proves that the promissory note was executed by the defendant, Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption that the instrument was made for consideration, which shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to establish that it is not supported by consideration [1].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. However, a contract whose consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as stated in the Exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, a fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom the fraud was practised or to whom the misrepresentation was made does not render a contract voidable under the Explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
capacity of parties to contract unsound mind disqualification
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
The National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 s6
rows.answer: Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject, as declared by Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12]. A person is considered to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time of making it, they are capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests, according to Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [2][12].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder homicide capital punishment life imprisonment death
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
Indian Penal Code section 302 murder
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s302
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
The CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE, 1973 s1
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life, according to Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [3].

In the Supreme Court judgment of Bharatkumar Rameshchandra Barot versus State of Gujarat, the Court modified a jail sentence and enhanced it by awarding the punishment of life imprisonment under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [2].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
punishment for theft Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft
Indian Penal Code section 379 punishment for theft
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s379
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Madhya Pradesh) [1][2][9]. 

In case of a second or subsequent conviction under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the punishment shall be rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and extending up to five years, with fine [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- Where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and a person is convicted for the first time, upon return of the value of property or restoration of the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

rows.question: What is the punishment for defamation?
queries: What is the punishment for defamation?
punishment for defamation criminal defamation imputation concerning any person intended to harm
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 356 defamation punishment
Indian Penal Code section 500 punishment for defamation
topSources: The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s500
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
The Indian Penal Code, 45 of 1860 (Rep., Act 45 of 2023) s499
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
rows.answer:
The punishment for defamation under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is simple imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, or fine, or both, or community service [1]. 

Related provisions:
- Section 356(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers whoever prints or engraves any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory of any person, with punishment of simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both [1].
- Section 356(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers whoever sells or offers for sale any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing that it contains such matter, with punishment of simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both [1].
- Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 covers punishment for defamation, providing that whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both [2].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
when person accused of non-bailable offence may be released on bail
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita section 480 bail in case of non-bailable offence

topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s480

rows.answer: A person accused of or suspected of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail when arrested or detained without a warrant by a police station officer in charge, or when appearing or brought before a court other than the High Court or Court of Session, except where there are reasonable grounds for believing the person is guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or is a previously convicted person as specified, unless an exception applies under the provisos for children, women, the sick or infirm, or other special reasons [1][2]. Additionally, if it appears at any stage of investigation, inquiry, or trial that there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed a non-bailable offence but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry, the accused shall be released on bail or on a bond [1][2]. In cases triable by a Magistrate where the trial for a non-bailable offence is not concluded within sixty days from the first date fixed for taking evidence while the accused is in custody throughout, the person shall be released on bail unless the Magistrate directs otherwise for reasons recorded in writing [1][2]. rows.question: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
queries: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?
application for setting aside arbitral award grounds limitation period
Arbitration and Conciliation Act section 34 application for setting aside arbitral award

An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, only if the party making the application establishes on the basis of the record of the arbitral tribunal that a party was under some incapacity; the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it or under the law for the time being in force; the party making the application was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case; the arbitral award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration, or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission (provided that separable matters can be partially set aside); or the composition of the arbitral tribunal or the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties or with Part I of the Act [1][11][12][13].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition and mode of transfer
Transfer of Property Act section 54 sale how made
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s58
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s38
rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, as stated in Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. To constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another, meaning all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, so that title passes from the seller to the buyer without the transferor retaining any part of their interest or right, according to the Supreme Court judgment in "Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others" [11].

Regarding how a sale is made and completed:
- In the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other intangible thing, a sale can be made only by a registered instrument, as provided in Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. rows.answer:
I couldn't find a direct or complete definition of all the inherent powers of a civil court in the sources I searched, but the sources mention the following regarding inherent powers:

- Nothing in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 shall limit or affect the inherent power of the Court to make orders necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court, as stated in Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [1].
- The competent authority and the appellate authority under the Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978 may exercise powers of the nature referred to in Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to the same extent and for the same purposes as such powers are exercisable by civil courts, according to Section 16B of the Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978 [3].

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
queries: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
punishment for identity theft using a computer or communication device
Information Technology Act section 66C punishment for identity theft
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 318 cheating by personation
topSources: The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016. s37
rows.answer:
- Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to rupees one lakh under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 66B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which covers punishment for dishonestly receiving stolen computer resource or communication device [6].
- Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which covers punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource [4].

rows.question: What is theft punishment?
queries: What is theft punishment?
theft punishment Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft

rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, and in case of a second or subsequent conviction, with rigorous imprisonment for a term of one to five years and with fine, under Section 303(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

For first-time convictions of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, upon the return or restoration of the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service, under Section 303(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].
